proposals.old:
Whether the gap between the implemented weight and the canonical one changes any reported result is a question the weight sweep of Section~\ref{sec:pareto} can answer in part. On Tiger the reward-maximizing tied bracket is $[0.01, 20]$ and on Diagnosis it is $[0.5, 20]$. Both weights, the implemented $w{=}1$ and the nat-canonical $0.69$ in the implementation's bit units, therefore lie inside it, and the choice of information base changes no qualitative conclusion there. On Bandit the tied bracket's grid endpoints are $[1, 2]$, which contains $w{=}1$ but not $0.69$. Because the sweep measures only grid weights, a weight that falls between two grid points is not directly observed, and $0.69$ falls between two of them. The nearest swept weight below it, $w{=}0.5$, scores $6.05$ against the tied $6.24$ (\texttt{results\_\allowbreak pareto\_\allowbreak sweep.csv}), so the sweep grid alone cannot say which side of that boundary the nat-canonical weight falls on.

To settle the remainder directly, we ran the exactly nat-canonical agent of Proposition~\ref{prop:equivalence}, $w{=}\ln 2$ in the implementation's bit units, together with a fresh $w{=}1$ run on the same seeds, under the sweep's own protocol (500 episodes $\times$ 5 seeds) on all five swept environments (\texttt{results\_\allowbreak nat\_\allowbreak canonical\_\allowbreak check.csv}, \url{experiments/run_nat_canonical_check.py}). On Tiger, Diagnosis, Bandit, and Testbed the two agents are bit-identical in reward, success rate, and mean observation count ($5.33$ and $99.6\%$ on Tiger, $-1.26$ and $97.4\%$ on Diagnosis, $6.24$ and $86.9\%$ on Bandit, $0.37$ and $96.4\%$ on Testbed). On four of the five swept environments, then, the choice of information base moves none of the sweep's reported numbers, and on Bandit in particular the nat-canonical weight lands inside the tied bracket rather than with $w{=}0.5$.

proposals.old: Deriving that recursion from a normalized preference distribution would add a term the recursion omits. Writing $Z = \sum_{o'} \exp(\beta R(o'))$ for the normalizer over the outcome space, $\ln P(o|C) = \beta R(o) - \ln Z$, and the constant $\ln Z$ is scored once per outcome, so a path that scores $T$ outcomes before it ends accumulates $-T \ln Z$. Observe-then-commit paths of different lengths score different numbers of outcomes, so that accumulated constant is policy-dependent and can change which of observing and committing minimizes the objective. Apart from the log-scoring case, in which the reward is itself a log probability so that $Z{=}1$ and the constant vanishes, it cancels only under a convention that scores the same number of outcomes on every path, for example a fixed-length construction in which an episode that has committed keeps emitting a null outcome of zero reward from an absorbing state at every remaining step, scored against one preference distribution over a common outcome space.
proposals.new: Deriving that recursion from a normalized preference distribution would add the accumulated term $-T\ln Z$ of Section~\ref{subsec:formal_rho_equiv}, which is policy-dependent because observe-then-commit paths score different numbers of outcomes. It vanishes under log scoring ($Z{=}1$) and otherwise cancels only when every path scores the same number of outcomes against one preference distribution over a common outcome space, for example when a committed episode keeps emitting a zero-reward null outcome from an absorbing state at every remaining step.
proposals.rationale: The normalizer derivation with its equation is stated in the main body (Section formal_rho_equiv). Keeps the appendix-only detail (the fixed-length null-outcome construction) and the scope sentence that follows.

proposals.old: The exact case is Bernardo's, where the reward is itself a log probability and no normalizer arises.
proposals.new: The exact case is that of \citet{bernardo1979}, where rewards are log scoring rules, so the reward is already a log probability measured in nats and no normalizer arises.
proposals.rationale: Absorbs the later, duplicated Bernardo sentence (removed in B20) at the first mention, with its citation.

proposals.old: The choice has a consequence for scale. Rescaling all rewards by a positive factor $k$ (the factor written $\alpha$ in Proposition~\ref{prop:pi1}) at fixed $w$ induces the same policy as weight $w/k$ on the unscaled rewards, so $w{=}1$ is not scale-invariant, and the reward-maximizing weight $w^*_{\mathrm{ret}}$ (the subscript abbreviates return) scales as $w^*_{\mathrm{ret}}(k)\propto k$ (Appendix~\ref{app:reward_scaling}). Following \citet{bernardo1979}, the identification is exact when rewards are log scoring rules, that is, when the reward for an outcome is the log probability the agent assigned to that outcome, so that reward is already measured in nats and no unit conversion stands between the two terms.

proposals.old:
The implementation measures information in bits rather than nats (\texttt{scipy.\allowbreak stats.\allowbreak entropy} with $\mathrm{base}{=}2$), a constant-factor difference that we make explicit here. Every result reported as EFE ($w{=}1$) in this article runs the agent at $w{=}1$ in those bit units, that is, one reward unit per bit. Since one bit is $\ln 2$ nats, one reward unit per bit is one reward unit per $\ln 2$ nats, or $1/\ln 2$ reward units per nat, which is an effective nat-denominated weight of $1/\ln 2 \approx 1.44$. Running the same conversion in reverse, the exactly canonical nat-unit identification of Proposition~\ref{prop:equivalence} corresponds to $w = \ln 2 \approx 0.69$ in the implementation's bit units.

Whether that constant factor changes any reported result is settled directly in Appendix~\ref{app:nat_canonical}, which runs the exactly nat-canonical agent of Proposition~\ref{prop:equivalence}, $w{=}\ln 2$ in the implementation's bit units, under the Pareto sweep protocol of Section~\ref{sec:pareto} on all five swept environments (\texttt{results\_\allowbreak nat\_\allowbreak canonical\_\allowbreak check.csv}). On Tiger, Diagnosis, Bandit, and Testbed it is bit-identical to the implemented $w{=}1$ agent in reward, success rate, and observation count. Where that sweep's mean reward is exactly tied across adjacent swept weights, its reward-maximizing weight is reported as the closed range of tied grid weights, the reward-maximizing tied bracket. On Tiger and Diagnosis both weights lie inside it, and on Bandit, whose bracket has grid endpoints $[1, 2]$ and so contains $w{=}1$ but not $0.69$, the directly run nat-canonical agent attains the bracket's tied reward. Tileworld is the one swept environment where the base changes the policy, and there $w{=}1$ remains Pareto-dominated by $w{=}20$ under either convention.
proposals.new: The implementation measures information in bits (\texttt{scipy.\allowbreak stats.\allowbreak entropy} with $\mathrm{base}{=}2$) and runs every reported EFE ($w{=}1$) agent at one reward unit per bit, which is $1/\ln 2 \approx 1.44$ reward units per nat. The exactly nat-canonical identification of Proposition~\ref{prop:equivalence} is therefore $w = \ln 2 \approx 0.69$ in the implementation's bit units. Appendix~\ref{app:nat_canonical} runs that agent on all five swept environments. It is bit-identical to the implemented $w{=}1$ agent in reward, success rate, and observation count on Tiger, Diagnosis, Bandit, and Testbed, and on Tileworld, the one environment where the base changes the policy, $w{=}1$ remains Pareto-dominated by $w{=}20$ under either convention.
proposals.rationale: Two paragraphs that restate the main body (Section formal_rho_equiv, the bit/nat paragraph) and Appendix nat_canonical nearly sentence for sentence. One paragraph keeps the conversion, the implementation pointer, and the per-environment consequences that Appendix line 2104 points here for. The tied-bracket definition moves to Appendix nat_canonical (B15).

proposals.old: Under a constant step, which no reported run uses, the recursion need not converge to a point. The standard constant-step stochastic-approximation intuition is that the iterate is instead held near $w^*$ in a neighborhood whose width shrinks with the step size, and that this residual motion is the mechanism that lets the controller re-adapt after the budget or environment shifts. Making it precise requires constant-step tracking arguments (stationary-distribution or moment bounds under drift and noise assumptions) that we do not develop here. Section~\ref{sec:dual_multiseed} assesses re-adaptation under reward-scale shift empirically on the decaying schedule, to which the same intuition applies through whatever step size is left at the moment of the shift. That section also runs the reset-on-shift variant, described next.
proposals.new: Under a constant step, which no reported run uses, the recursion need not converge to a point. The standard intuition that the iterate instead stays in a step-size-dependent neighborhood of $w^*$, which would let the controller re-adapt after a shift, would require constant-step tracking arguments that we do not develop. Section~\ref{sec:dual_multiseed} assesses re-adaptation under reward-scale shift empirically on the decaying schedule, together with the reset-on-shift variant described next.
proposals.rationale: Same scope statement (no tracking guarantee, re-adaptation empirical only) in fewer words.

proposals.old: Their method is not a Lagrangian one. Point-based solvers represent the value function by a set of vectors over beliefs and discard the dominated ones at each backup, and their method enforces the cost bound inside that pruning step rather than pricing it. The dominated vectors are pruned exactly with a minimax quadratically constrained program and approximately with a linear program at each collected belief point.
proposals.new: Their method is not a Lagrangian one. It enforces the cost bound inside the point-based pruning of dominated value vectors at each collected belief point, exactly with a minimax quadratically constrained program or approximately with a linear program, rather than pricing it.

proposals.old: We do not have such a solver, so Section~\ref{sec:cpomdp} benchmarks against a near-optimal constrained-POMDP reference on the three core observe-then-commit environments (Tiger, Diagnosis, and Bandit). The reference is built as a Lagrangian-penalized sweep. For each value of a penalty $\lambda$ on a grid, the POMDP is re-solved by SARSOP, the offline point-based solver that already serves as this paper's near-optimal reference (Section~\ref{sec:sarsop}), with every observation action charged an extra $\lambda$. The reward and usage of the resulting policy are then estimated by Monte Carlo simulation. SARSOP is solved to precision $10^{-3}$, and the reference is a simulation estimate rather than a certified exact solution. Because a near-optimal reference is a feasible policy rather than a certified optimum, it can only estimate the constrained optimum from below, up to its own sampling error and the upward selection bias of taking a maximum over noisy sampled points, so any measured gap to it understates the gap to the optimum up to those two effects. The estimated optimality gap, the gap between the EFE agent at $w{=}1$ and this reference, is small, zero on Tiger and within Monte Carlo noise of zero on Bandit and Diagnosis.
proposals.new: We do not have such a solver, so Section~\ref{sec:cpomdp} benchmarks against a near-optimal constrained-POMDP reference on Tiger, Diagnosis, and Bandit, the feasible envelope of a SARSOP usage-penalty sweep evaluated by Monte Carlo simulation (Appendix~\ref{app:cpomdp_details}). It is a feasible-policy estimate rather than a certified optimum, so up to its own sampling error and the upward selection bias of maximizing over noisy points it estimates the constrained optimum from below, and any measured gap to it understates the gap to the optimum. The estimated gap between the EFE agent at $w{=}1$ and this reference is zero on Tiger and small relative to the estimates' standard errors on Diagnosis and Bandit.
proposals.rationale: The penalized-sweep construction is described in full in Section cpomdp and Appendix cpomdp_details. The appendix copy also described the reference as the raw penalized sweep, while the reference is the LP feasible envelope over sampled points. The rewrite matches Section cpomdp's wording ('small relative to the estimates' standard errors') and keeps the selection-bias and understatement caveats.

proposals.old: The RockSample[7,8] reference calculation instead exposes a limitation. We apply the usage-cap Lagrangian construction of Section~\ref{sec:cpomdp}, a per-observation penalty of $\lambda$, to this project's own depth-3 tree search (the reference planner for RockSample, standing in for SARSOP) and sweep the same log-spaced 12-point $\lambda$ grid used there for the three core environments (\url{experiments/run_rocksample_cpomdp_reference.py}). The result is a degenerate frontier, the reward-versus-usage curve that the sweep traces collapsing to two points. Across the entire lambda range the penalized planner checks zero or one rock, reward $9.5$ or $12.3$, and never approaches EFE's actual operating point of $9.84$ checks, so no meaningful reference reward is available there. The failure is structural rather than a tuning artifact. A literal usage-cap penalty rewards a check only through what a 3-step lookahead can see beyond it. No such short horizon can justify checking eight rocks in sequence, whereas the information-floor dual that Planning+IG and EFE actually use credits each check's information gain immediately at the node where it occurs, independent of horizon. The usage-cap Lagrangian that gives a near-optimal reference on Tiger, Diagnosis, and Bandit relies on SARSOP's effectively unbounded horizon, and it has no depth-limited analogue that reaches RockSample's operating region. Closing this gap remains future work with a sharper target, either a genuinely deeper RockSample solver or a usage-cap construction that values information locally the way the information-floor dual already does.
proposals.new: No constrained reference is available for RockSample. Applying the same per-observation penalty $\lambda$ over the same 12-point grid to this project's depth-3 tree search on RockSample[7,8] (\url{experiments/run_rocksample_cpomdp_reference.py}) gives a planner that checks zero or one rock at every $\lambda$, at reward $9.5$ or $12.3$, far from EFE's $9.84$ checks. A usage penalty credits a check only through what a 3-step lookahead sees beyond it, whereas the information weight credits each check's information gain at the node where it occurs, so the penalty construction depends on SARSOP's effectively unbounded horizon. A deeper RockSample solver, or a usage-cap construction that values information locally, would be needed.
proposals.rationale: Compresses a failed reference attempt to the scope limit the main body relies on (Section budget_positioning: 'The shallow RockSample reference fails to reach EFE's operating region. Appendix theory_positioning reports that limitation'). Keeps the script, the numbers, and the structural reason.

proposals.old: What it buys instead is twofold. The design primitive becomes a quantity a practitioner can actually state (a sensing budget in observation count or cost) rather than one they must guess. The online dual controller (Proposition~\ref{prop:pi5}) skips the offline curve entirely, converging from interaction alone to the budget crossing point. Scale equivariance (Proposition~\ref{prop:pi1}) lets a count-usage curve computed at one reward scale transfer across pure reward-and-cost rescalings without recomputation, and lets a cost-usage curve transfer after rescaling by the same factor. That is a property of the planner and its weight rather than of how the weight was chosen. The same transformation carries a directly tuned weight $w$ to $\alpha w$ under the same rescaling and tie-break assumptions, on a weight grid rescaled with the rewards, as the scaling of the reward-optimal tuned weights in Section~\ref{subsec:formal_rho_equiv} already records.
proposals.new: What it buys instead is a design primitive a practitioner can state (a sensing budget in observation count or cost) rather than a weight they must guess, and an online controller (Proposition~\ref{prop:pi5}) that skips the offline curve and, under that proposition's conditions, converges from interaction alone to the budget crossing point. Scale equivariance (Proposition~\ref{prop:pi1}) lets a count-usage curve computed at one reward scale transfer across pure reward-and-cost rescalings without recomputation, and a cost-usage curve transfer after rescaling by the same factor. That is a property of the planner and its weight, not of how the weight was chosen, and it carries a directly tuned weight $w$ to $\alpha w$ under the same rescaling and tie-break assumptions, on a weight grid rescaled with the rewards (Section~\ref{subsec:formal_rho_equiv}).
proposals.rationale: Also fixes an internal miscount ('twofold' followed by three items) and conditions the controller's convergence on Proposition PI-5's hypotheses, matching the claim-calibration vocabulary.
